rows.arm_result: no clinical result reported; descriptive histology only: the text says tattoo-device needles create 'turbulent whirling of the drug that increases its dermal diffusion', while the figure legend says 'the extensive pigment diffusion are larger with the handheld needle' [direction of the difference unclear]
rows.uncertainty: Excluded from Module 1 analysis: letter with no IGH patients and no clinical outcome; the ex vivo model used black ink, not 5-fluorouracil, on non-IGH abdominoplasty skin. Internal conflict: the body text argues the tattoo machine increases dermal diffusion, but the Fig 1 legend states the 'extensive pigment diffusion are larger with the handheld needle'; images not reviewed (figure not in saved text). Number of skin fragments, sections or repeats not reported; no quantification. Safety statements ('likely safe', 'may also minimize the adverse effects') are opinion without data. Conflict of interest: first author owns Traderm, which sells tattoo machines and cartridges; a co-author is his daughter; funding footnote names Traderm. An IRB approval number is given although no patient study is described. Claims about speed, anesthesia and reproducibility are the authors' views, not measured. Leads: ref 2 (arbache2018) and ref 4 (Int J Dermatol 2019 drug-delivery study) are the primary sources for the protocol.
rows.citation: Arbache S, de Mendonça MT, Arbache ST, Hirata SH. Treatment of idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis with a tattoo device versus a handheld needle. JAAD Int 2021;3:14-16
